title: Restoration of nephron endowment after the nephrogenic clock stops

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to restart nephron production inside a human kidney after developmental nephrogenesis has ended. Nephrons are the kidney’s filtering units. Success would require recreating the progenitor cells and supporting niche that build them, then producing new units that receive blood, filter it and drain their filtrate into the collecting system. The pediatric target is restoration of a developmentally deficient nephron endowment.

The defining boundary is cessation of developmental nephrogenesis, rather than birth. Some preterm infants continue making nephrons after delivery. Preserving that ongoing process, repairing cells within existing nephrons and growing kidney tissue in a dish are relevant advances, but each differs from restarting production after the developmental program has stopped. This concept requires a lasting addition of integrated, functioning nephrons to the kidney.

significance.text: Developmental nephrogenesis normally finishes near the end of human gestation. After cessation, the supplied literature describes a nephron population that is not replenished and can decline through ageing or disease. Preterm birth and fetal growth restriction can reduce nephron endowment and are associated with greater risk of chronic kidney disease later in life. These are risk relationships, not evidence that every affected infant has the same deficit or eventual outcome.

Safely adding a clinically meaningful cohort of functioning nephrons after this developmental limit would create a major regenerative capability: expansion of the kidney’s functional endowment after its original production period. The anticipated direct benefit would be additional filtering capacity. Restoring normal lifetime filtration reserve is a stronger, conditional possibility requiring sufficient nephron number, appropriate maturation, durable integration and protection against later disease; it does not follow automatically from an initial increase in filtration.

Conditional synthesis: the clearest initial application would be children with documented low endowment and a kidney environment capable of supporting new tissue. Extension to scarred adult kidneys would require additional advances in the damaged tissue environment. Reopening nephron production should therefore not be equated with a general cure for chronic kidney disease or a guarantee that later transplantation would never be needed.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the supplied literature is reconstruction of a productive nephrogenic niche after the original progenitor population and its supporting environment have disappeared. Little and Humphreys describe developmental progenitor exhaustion, including disappearance of the nephrogenic zone within two days of birth in mice. That mouse timing illustrates the developmental shutdown; it should not be transferred directly to human infants.

Generating recognizable nephron structures is only part of the engineering problem. New nephrons must mature, acquire a functional blood supply and maintain open connections to urinary drainage. They must also be produced at sufficient scale to change kidney function. The 2022 review identifies nephron number, effective renal capacity and anatomical organization as major shortcomings of human pluripotent stem cell-derived kidney tissue compared with a mature organ.

Engineering synthesis: an intervention would need to coordinate progenitor maintenance with orderly differentiation, control where new tissue forms and stop growth when the intended amount has been produced. It would also need to avoid tumors and malformed collecting-system connections. A separate measurement barrier is proving that treatment created additional nephrons: improved kidney function alone could reflect maturation, enlargement or repair of existing units.

current_state.text: Sutherland and Black’s review, published online on 16 January 2023, states that humans born at term reach maximal nephron number when nephrogenesis finishes, at approximately 36 weeks’ gestation, and that nephron number subsequently remains stable until losses occur through ageing or disease. The supplied review had access to the PubMed abstract record, rather than the full article, so the retained evidence supports these broad statements without establishing the article’s complete discussion.

Carpenter, Yarlagadda, VandenHeuvel, Ding and Schuh’s study in the February 2024 issue of Kidney International Reports examined seven preterm infants who survived more than 40 days and eight controls. Four of the seven preterm infants had histologic and molecular evidence of ongoing nephrogenesis, and the article reports persistence up to 62 postnatal days. Cessation was earlier than in postmenstrual-age-matched controls but remained within the usual 32-to-36-week postmenstrual-age window. This small observational autopsy study documents developmental continuation after birth; it does not demonstrate treatment-induced restarting after cessation or establish the eventual functional contribution of those nephrons. The supplied review assessed article text obtained through full-text XML; figures and supplementary images were not inspected.

Little and Humphreys’ January 2022 review reports no evidence of new nephron generation in postnatal mammalian kidneys in its discussion of adult kidney stem cells and regeneration. Read literally across every postnatal developmental stage, that statement would conflict with continued nephrogenesis in preterm infants and with the review’s own mouse developmental timing. Its relevant interpretation here is the absence of demonstrated regeneration after developmental nephrogenesis has ended. The review also describes filtration in transplanted organoid tissue, a partial achievement that does not by itself establish sufficient nephron scale, complete urinary drainage or restoration of native kidney endowment.

The research notes cite a Development paper dated 25 May 2021 and attribute to it a mouse experiment in which excess GDNF prolonged the progenitor program by a few postnatal days without increasing glomerular density above the late-embryonic level. No source text for that paper was retained in the supplied evidence. The duration, experimental conditions and density comparison therefore remain unverified here. The reported observation remains relevant as a possible example of prolonging development, but it cannot establish restarting after cessation; glomerular density also should not be treated as interchangeable with total nephron number or functional capacity.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material does not demonstrate a durable addition of connected, filtering human nephrons after verified cessation of nephrogenesis. Its dated findings support the biological rationale and the distinction between developmental continuation and regeneration. Because the supplied freshness record contains no search evidence, they do not establish an exhaustive account of achievements through 1 November 2026. The missing GDNF source likewise limits assessment of that experiment without showing that its reported findings are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed preclinical demonstration: treat a large mammal only after verifying that developmental nephrogenesis has ceased. Show a measured and lasting increase in newly formed nephrons that are vascularized, filter and connect to urinary drainage. Before treatment, define a clinically important endowment deficit and a substantial fraction of it that the intervention aims to close. These are proposed criteria, not established completion standards.
completion_criteria.label: Lasting functional nephron addition in large mammals after nephrogenesis ceases

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional and safety demonstration: show that added nephron formation produces a filtration benefit that persists beyond the growth period, alongside evidence that existing nephrons’ maturation, hypertrophy or repair cannot explain the result. Prespecify follow-up duration and surveillance for tumors and disordered collecting-system anatomy. Finding no such events during that interval would establish an observed safety boundary, rather than permanent freedom from those risks.
completion_criteria.label: Added nephrons sustain filtration benefits beyond the growth period

completion_criteria.text: Proposed human demonstration: in children with documented low endowment, combine improved kidney function with validated imaging or tissue evidence capable of distinguishing additional nephron formation from changes in existing units. A function increase or an isolated biopsy finding would be insufficient on its own. Measurement methods would need to establish both the presence of new nephrons and a credible estimate of their contribution across the kidney.
completion_criteria.label: Validated evidence establishes new nephrons’ contribution to pediatric kidney improvement

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the result independently, with appropriate comparison groups, and define the ages, deficit causes, tissue conditions and treatment scales over which benefit is demonstrated. Establish that delivery, growth control and follow-up are feasible for the intended pediatric population. Finite studies would demonstrate performance within those tested conditions; claims of normal lifetime reserve or applicability to scarred adult kidneys would require further evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes pediatric benefit boundaries and treatment feasibility

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with PED-01, Physiological extrauterine support through fetal organ maturity: continued gestational support might preserve nephrogenesis while its developmental machinery is still active. PED-08 instead targets restoration after that machinery has ceased operating. These could address different stages of the same developmental vulnerability, but no PED-01 evidence was supplied to establish an effect of artificial-placenta support on nephron endowment.

Conceptual comparison with PED-04, Controlled reopening of developmental critical periods: both involve recovering a capability normally confined to a developmental interval. PED-08 specifically requires rebuilding a progenitor niche and producing anatomically integrated filtering units. The shared timing analogy does not establish a common mechanism or show that reopening a developmental window alone would be sufficient.

Conceptual comparison with PED-06, Prenatal correction that lets severe monogenic disease develop normally, and PED-11, One-time in vivo correction of severe newborn metabolic disease before irreversible injury: these roster entries emphasize early correction before developmental disruption or injury becomes established. PED-08 concerns adding organ units after their normal production period. Correcting an underlying genetic or metabolic cause would not itself demonstrate restoration of a missing nephron complement.

Conceptual comparison with PED-09, Post-symptomatic restoration of severe genetic neurodevelopmental disorders: both seek recovery after a developmental deficit has already emerged. Their required outcomes remain distinct: PED-08 demands additional connected, filtering nephrons, whereas the roster describes PED-09 in terms of neurodevelopmental restoration. Similar restorative ambition does not imply interchangeable biology or evidence.

Conceptual comparison with PED-12, Drug-free donor-specific tolerance for pediatric solid-organ grafts: PED-12 addresses immune acceptance of transplanted organs, while PED-08 addresses nephron production and functional integration. A donor-derived tissue approach could make immune tolerance relevant, but immune acceptance alone would not solve nephron scale, maturation or drainage. The concepts remain separate even if a future treatment combines them.

The closest technical overlaps outside the roster are developmental nephrology, progenitor reprogramming and kidney organoid engineering. Organoids offer a route to generating nephron-containing tissue, and transplanted organoid filtration is a relevant partial achievement. PED-08 requires the further demonstration that newly produced units durably expand a kidney’s functional endowment after developmental cessation.

change_log.change: Replaced birth as the decisive cutoff with verified cessation of developmental nephrogenesis.
change_log.reason: The supplied preterm-infant study documents continued nephrogenesis after delivery, including persistence up to 62 postnatal days.

change_log.change: Preserved the seven-infant cohort, four positive cases, 62-day observation and 32-to-36-week postmenstrual window, and added the eight controls and observational autopsy design.
change_log.reason: These details establish the finding’s scope and prevent developmental continuation from being mistaken for an intervention that restarts nephrogenesis.

change_log.change: Replaced guaranteed normal lifetime filtration reserve with added functional capacity and conditional longer-term restoration.
change_log.reason: Lifetime normalization requires evidence of sufficient scale, maturation, durability and subsequent disease protection.

change_log.change: Interpreted the 2022 postnatal-regeneration statement in its adult kidney stem-cell context.
change_log.reason: A literal denial of all postnatal nephrogenesis would conflict with the supplied human observations and mouse developmental timing.

change_log.change: Retained the reported GDNF experiment with explicit attribution and uncertainty.
change_log.reason: No source artifact was supplied to verify its duration or density result; that limitation does not establish that the report is false.

change_log.change: Integrated organoid filtration as a partial achievement and expanded the scale, vascularization, maturation and urinary-drainage barriers.
change_log.reason: The review distinguishes functioning transplanted tissue from clinically sufficient restoration of integrated nephron endowment.

change_log.change: Strengthened proposed demonstrations with verified pretreatment cessation, prespecified deficit targets, discrimination from existing-nephron changes, bounded safety follow-up and independent replication.
change_log.reason: These additions make the proposal assessable without presenting proposed thresholds as standards or finite observations as proof of lifelong safety.

change_log.change: Preserved abstract-only access, uninspected figures and supplements, the missing GDNF text and the absence of freshness evidence.
change_log.reason: These limitations affect how confidently the dated literature can support individual claims and present-day conclusions.

change_log.change: Retained PED-01 as a qualified conceptual comparison and added relevant roster distinctions.
change_log.reason: The supplied roster supports conceptual relationships, but no evidence was supplied for artificial-placenta effects on nephron endowment or shared mechanisms across entries.

unresolved_issues: Whether any work through 1 November 2026 demonstrates restoration after verified cessation remains unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The 2021 GDNF experiment’s methods, duration, total nephron effects and reported glomerular-density comparison cannot be assessed without retained source text.
A validated, practically usable method for quantifying newly formed functional nephrons across a living human kidney is not established in the supplied material.
The clinically important deficit, target fraction to restore, minimum functional benefit and required follow-up duration remain to be defined.
The ages, causes of low endowment and tissue conditions compatible with successful niche reconstruction remain unknown.
Normal lifetime filtration reserve and benefit in scarred adult kidneys require evidence beyond the proposed initial demonstrations.
The effect of PED-01 extrauterine support on nephrogenesis was not assessed in the supplied evidence.

brief.title: New kidney filters after natural production stops
possible: Children whose kidneys developed too few filters could gain new ones after the normal production period has ended. These filters, called nephrons, would grow inside the kidney, receive blood, filter it and drain into the kidney’s urine collection system.
why: The number of nephrons a child starts with helps determine how much blood their kidneys can filter and how well they withstand disease. Premature birth and restricted growth before birth can leave children with fewer nephrons and a greater risk of kidney disease later in life.

Adding working nephrons would increase filtering capacity for children with a documented shortfall. It would give medicine a way to expand that capacity after the kidney’s original building period has closed.

sources.who: Megan R Sutherland and Mary Jane Black
sources.showed: Their review describes how nephron numbers stop increasing when development ends, and how premature birth and restricted fetal growth can reduce the starting supply.
sources.quote: The number of nephrons does not increase further and subsequently remains stable until loss occurs through ageing or disease.
sources.cited_for: A low starting supply can affect kidney health throughout life.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a treatment that restarts nephron production.

sources.who: James Carpenter, Sunitha Yarlagadda, Katherine A VandenHeuvel, Lili Ding and M P Schuh
sources.showed: A small autopsy study found that some premature infants continued making nephrons after birth.
sources.quote: On histologic examination, we found that some, but not all, preterm infants continue nephrogenesis postnatally, for up to 62 days, longer than is conventionally believed.
sources.cited_for: Birth does not necessarily mark the end of nephron production.
sources.not_established: Continued development does not demonstrate restarting production after it has stopped.

sources.who: Melissa H Little and Benjamin D Humphreys
sources.showed: Their review describes filtration in transplanted organoids, small kidney-like tissues grown from stem cells. It also identifies gaps in their scale and organization.
sources.cited_for: Lab-grown kidney tissue offers partial progress toward building working nephrons.
sources.not_established: Filtering tissue does not establish lasting additions to a kidney with complete urine drainage after development ends.

sources.showed: This is a mouse experiment on prolonging developmental nephron production.
sources.cited_for: Prolonging development is a distinct step from restarting it.
sources.not_established: Prolonged production does not establish new, functioning nephrons after production has ceased.

shown: Carpenter and colleagues found continued nephron production in some premature infants in a small autopsy study. Little and Humphreys describe filtration in transplanted lab-grown kidney tissue. Neither demonstrates lasting additions of connected, working nephrons inside a human kidney after natural production has stopped.
missing: Researchers have yet to rebuild the starter cells and supporting environment that make nephrons after that developmental system disappears.
New nephrons must gain blood flow, mature and connect to urine drainage in numbers large enough to improve kidney function.
Growth must stop at the intended amount without tumors or malformed drainage connections.
Measurements must distinguish added nephrons from repair, enlargement or maturation of existing filters.

milestones.label: Lasting new filters in large mammals after production stops
milestones.explanation: Treatment would have to durably replace a predefined, substantial share of a meaningful deficit with new filters that receive blood and drain urine after confirmed shutdown in large mammals. This would establish functional rebuilding.

milestones.label: Added filters sustain benefits beyond growth
milestones.explanation: Added filters would have to sustain filtration gains beyond growth, with existing filters unable to explain them and defined monitoring for tumors and abnormal drainage. This would establish durability and observed safety limits.

milestones.label: New filters explain improved kidney function in children
milestones.explanation: Children with documented shortages would need improved function plus validated imaging or tissue measurements of new filters and their contribution across the kidney. This would connect the benefit to added filters.

milestones.label: Independent studies establish who benefits and treatment feasibility
milestones.explanation: Independent studies with comparison groups would have to reproduce benefit, define suitable children and kidney conditions, and establish feasible delivery, growth control and follow-up. This would define where treatment works.

uncertain: The size of a meaningful nephron shortfall, the fraction to replace and the necessary benefit and follow-up remain undefined.
Which ages, causes of low nephron numbers and kidney tissue conditions would support rebuilding remain unknown.
An initial filtration gain would not establish normal lifelong reserve or benefit in scarred adult kidneys.

page.title: Human nephrogenesis after developmental cessation
page.definition: A human kidney resumes nephron formation after its developmental programme has ended. The new nephrons—blood-filtering units—add to nephron number, receive blood, filter plasma and drain filtrate into the kidney’s collecting system.

goal.need: Human nephrogenesis usually ends at about 36 weeks’ gestation, after which nephron losses are not replaced. Prematurity and restricted fetal growth can reduce nephron endowment. A Swedish cohort followed 4,186,615 singleton births during 1973–2014 through 31 December 2015; 4,305 people received a chronic kidney disease diagnosis. The associations below quantify population risk, rather than an individual nephron deficit.

figures.caption: Chronic kidney disease by gestational age at birth, ages 0–43 years
figures.note: Extremely preterm births are included in the preterm category. These associations do not measure nephron number.

statements.quote: in vivo regeneration of functional nephrons
statements.context: RFA-DK-14-010 identifies this as a direction for the ReBuilding a Kidney research network, alongside generating nephrons outside the body for transplantation.

statements.body: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
statements.quote: Develop an understanding of in vivo kidney regeneration and test novel ways to increase nephron number or nephron function.
statements.context: A research objective in RFA-DK-19-007. The objective does not specifically require restarting nephrogenesis after developmental cessation.

completion.title: A human kidney forms filtering, draining nephrons after developmental nephrogenesis has ended.
completion.criterion: After documented cessation of developmental nephrogenesis in a human kidney, an intervention initiates new nephron formation and increases total nephron number. The additional units remain present at follow-up, receive blood, filter plasma and drain filtrate into that kidney’s collecting system. Evidence distinguishes new units from developmental continuation, repair and enlargement of existing nephrons.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside completion test specifically for restarting nephrogenesis after developmental cessation was located.
completion.basis: Searches covered NIDDK RBK solicitations and reports, Kidney Health Initiative roadmap material, FDA guidance, ClinicalTrials.gov and kidney-regeneration consensus literature. No post-cessation completion criterion was located. NIDDK supplies the functional integration requirements of filtration and collecting-system drainage. The fallback adds initiation after verified cessation, distinguishing this capability from prolonged development.

milestones.title: Human stem cells form organoids containing contiguous podocyte, proximal and distal nephron segments.
milestones.criterion: Human pluripotent stem cells form organoids—three-dimensional tissues grown in culture—with cells resembling podocytes, proximal tubules and distal tubules in contiguous, proximodistally patterned segments, supported by morphology and segment-specific markers. This is a descriptive identification convention, without a consensus organoid definition or minimum nephron count. NIDDK’s January 2019 report describes organoids with identifiable nephron segments.
milestones.set_by: Kidney-organoid research community, as summarized by Freedman and Dekel in 2023; a descriptive identification convention rather than an agreed functional standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: cells resembling podocytes, proximal tubules, and distal tubules in contiguous segments patterned along a proximal-to-distal axis

milestones.title: New kidney tissue filters blood and drains filtrate into a host kidney collecting system.
milestones.criterion: New kidney tissue demonstrates both blood filtration and drainage of the resulting filtrate into a host kidney collecting system. NIDDK states this integration challenge without a numerical filtration or duration threshold. A review published online on 19 November 2024 reports filtration in transplanted organoids but no apparent route for filtrate excretion; it documents only part of this result.
milestones.set_by: NIDDK, Recent Advances & Emerging Opportunities 2019, Iain Drummond’s RBK scientific presentation, page 98; the challenge concerns engrafted kidney tissue.
milestones.threshold_quote: blood filtration (cleansing) and drainage into a host kidney collecting system.

milestones.title: A mammalian kidney forms additional nephrons after its developmental nephrogenesis has ended.
milestones.criterion: An intervention begun after developmental nephrogenesis has ceased initiates nephron formation within a mammalian kidney and increases its total nephron number. Li et al., published on 25 May 2021, found nephron precursors at postnatal day 7 in GDNF-altered mice (n=3 kidneys), showing developmental prolongation. Tajima et al., published on 28 February 2022, found glomerular and tubular structures in implanted pig-kidney matrix after 28 days (kidney morphometry, n=4); a whole-kidney nephron-number increase was not established.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of RBK objectives and nephrogenesis literature located no published preclinical pass criterion specifically requiring initiation after cessation.

milestones.title: New segmented nephrons form inside a human kidney after developmental nephrogenesis has ended.
milestones.criterion: After documented cessation of developmental nephrogenesis, an intervention initiates new segmented nephron formation inside a human kidney. This anatomical result precedes demonstration of integrated filtration and drainage. Carpenter et al., published on 4 November 2023, studied autopsy tissue from 7 preterm infants surviving more than 40 days and 8 controls; 4 of the 7 showed ongoing nephrogenesis. That observation demonstrates developmental continuation.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; no registered human protocol with an endpoint establishing post-cessation nephron formation was located.

not_found: Published numerical requirements for added nephron number, filtration gain and follow-up duration were not located.
No human result demonstrating post-cessation nephron formation with both filtration and collecting-system drainage was located.
The supplied Little–Humphreys full text could not be reopened because PMC returned a browser check.
